bamboo_species.description: Culms grow in clumps, erect with an out-arching crown up to 20m tall. Nodes are dipping with glabrous green internodes up to 49cm long and 8.25cm in diameter. The culm wall is 3.0cm thick at the base, becoming thinner toward the top.
bamboo_species.habitat: Commonly planted in settled areas at low and medium altitudes.
bamboo_species.distribution: Native to Java and Eastern Malesia; cultivated in Southern China, Malay Peninsula, Moluccas, and the Philippines (Northern Luzon to Mindanao).
bamboo_species.economic_importance: Top to bottom of culms are used for musical instruments. It is also used in building construction, furniture, kitchen utensils, and papermaking; young shoots are edible.

bamboo_species.description: Open clumps with about 30 erect, straight, or slightly zigzag culms up to 15m tall. Internodes are bluish-green, shining, and slightly grooved on the branch side.
bamboo_species.distribution: Originated in tropical Asia; pantropically cultivated. In the Philippines, it is found from Northern Luzon to Palawan and Mindanao.
bamboo_species.economic_importance: Classified as soft bamboo used in light construction, pulp, paper, and handicrafts.
bamboo_species.distinguishing_features: Glabrous shining bluish-green culms and sulcate internodes.

bamboo_species.scientific_name: Cyrtochloa hirsuta S Dransf. sp. nov.
bamboo_species.description: Culms are 6-7m tall, green turning yellow at maturity, with thin walls and internodes 50-70cm long. The tips are long and drooping.
bamboo_species.economic_importance: Used locally for fences, barbecue sticks, and agricultural implements due to thin walls.
bamboo_species.distinguishing_features: Thin culm wall, long internodes, and rigid foliage leaves.

bamboo_species.scientific_name: Dendrocalamus asper (Schultes f.) Backer ex Heyne
bamboo_species.description: Large culms reaching over 20m tall with diameters of 12-16cm near the base. Covered with velvety brown hairs when young.
bamboo_species.habitat: Grows well from low altitudes up to 1500m.
bamboo_species.distribution: Planted throughout Southeast Asia; introduced in Philippine bambusetums in Mt. Makiling and Bukidnon.
bamboo_species.economic_importance: Used in house construction, plywood, and tiles; young shoots are edible.
bamboo_species.distinguishing_features: Densely persistent brown velvety hairs covering lower internodes and swollen nodes with many aerial roots.

bamboo_species.description: Sturdy culms up to 20m tall with green, smooth internodes. Walls are up to 4.0cm thick, often nearly solid at the base.
bamboo_species.habitat: Generally planted in settled areas; prefers deep fertile soil.
bamboo_species.distribution: Endemic to various provinces in Luzon, Leyte, Cebu, Bohol, and Mindanao.
bamboo_species.economic_importance: Preferred for furniture making (vehicle shafts, yokes), building construction, ropes, and papermaking.

synonyms: Bambusa thouarsii Kunth var. atter Hassk.
bamboo_species.description: Culms 12-25m tall, closely tufted. Young culms are powdery waxy with bluish-green internodes.
bamboo_species.habitat: Thrives in tropics up to 1400m altitude.
bamboo_species.distribution: Originated in Java; cultivated in Davao and Laguna in the Philippines.
bamboo_species.economic_importance: Culms used for building materials, household utensils, handicrafts, and banana props; shoots are edible.

bamboo_species.description: Clumps of 10-22 culms up to 20m tall. Internodes are 15-30cm long, hollow with walls 1-3cm thick. Culm sheaths are densely hairy dark-brown when young.
bamboo_species.habitat: All clumps are cultivated or naturalized.
bamboo_species.distribution: Native to the Philippines (Luzon, Leyte, Camiguin de Misamis, etc.).
bamboo_species.economic_importance: Culms are used for various musical instruments, building construction, basketry, and furniture; shoots are edible.

bamboo_species.description: Closely tufted culms up to 30m tall. Internodes are green with a prominent white-waxy bloom, 20.5–54.5cm long.
bamboo_species.distribution: Originated from Java; cultivated in Davao.
bamboo_species.economic_importance: Used for roofs, handicrafts, water containers, and fibers for clothes in Indonesia.

bamboo_species.description: Forms large clumps with 240–370 slender culms. Internodes are hollow and green, with fine irritating hairs when young.
bamboo_species.habitat: Thickets and secondary forests at low to medium altitudes.
bamboo_species.distribution: Philippines (Luzon to Basilan), New Guinea, Solomon Islands, and Sulawesi.
bamboo_species.economic_importance: Ideal for sawali boards; shoots are edible. Historically used to polish brass.
bamboo_species.distinguishing_features: Similar to S. lumampao but with smaller culms; internodes have sandpapery hairs.

bamboo_species.description: Clumps up to 3m in diameter with ~200 culms, 10-11m tall. Internodes are 60-90cm long with thin walls (0.17cm at top).
bamboo_species.habitat: Thickets and secondary forests at low and medium altitudes.
bamboo_species.distribution: Endemic to various Philippine islands (Luzon to Basilan).
bamboo_species.economic_importance: Culms used for musical instruments, sawali, baskets, and spears.
bamboo_species.distinguishing_features: Generally larger culms than S. lima in natural habitats.

bamboo_species.description: A high-climbing tropical genus with zigzag culms found in hill forests. Culms are solid or have a small lumen and twine around tree trunks.
Mature culms are distant from each other. Young culms have distinctive silvery white pubescence on nodes and internodes. Internodes are very long (up to 80cm).
bamboo_species.habitat: Grows well in cool climates or high altitudes up to 1600m.
bamboo_species.distribution: Warm-temperate China; recently introduced to the Philippines for experimental purposes.
bamboo_species.economic_importance: Culms used for flutes; major commercial species in China/Japan for building and food.
instruments: Pulala or Hulagteb (long flute of the Talaandig tribe)

from_the_field.title: From the Field
from_the_field.subtitle: Where Philippine instrument bamboos grow and are harvested.

sections.title: Lowland Stands
sections.content: Clumps generally planted in settled areas across Luzon, Leyte, Cebu, and Bohol. Its sturdy, thick-walled culms, which can grow up to 20 meters, serve as primary material for instruments like the Unnat jaw harp.

sections.title: Hillside
sections.bamboo: Buho Thin-walled Anos (Schizostachyum lima) and Lumampao (S. lumampao)
sections.content: Harvested from secondary forests and thickets at low to medium altitudes. These species are the preferred choice for King Flute panpipes and the Tungali nose flutes of the Cordilleras due to their ideal diameter and hollow structure.

sections.title: Giant Bamboo Grove
sections.content: Cultivated in groves up to 1,500 meters altitude. With culms reaching over 20 meters and diameters up to 16 centimeters, it provides the massive resonators needed for T’boli barrel drums (Tnonggong) and the bodies of modern engineered bamboo guitars.

sections.title: Cordillera Highlands
sections.content: Mountain stands feed the rich musical traditions of the Kalinga and Majukayong tribes. These highland bamboos are meticulously air-dried for at least a week to prepare them for the intricate skin-carving required for Kullibit zithers.

sections.title: Harvest Season
sections.content: Artisans observe traditional environmental indicators; Aeta makers harvest one-year-old “tinaunan” culms during the summer to prevent cracking, while Bagobo-Tagabawa elders harvest only during “dulom” (moonless nights) to protect the wood from “bukbok” (powder-post beetle) and fungal damage.

sections.title: Sustainable Supply
sections.content: The BMI Innovation R&D Program utilizes science to characterization and digitize bamboo species to ensure a standardized supply for the industry. This program aims to support the increased demand caused by the inclusion of bamboo music in the national K-12 curriculum.

sections.title: Sustainable Harvest
sections.content: A regenerative cycle where bamboo is chosen for its endless renewability as a natural resource. Producers like Huni Ukulele emphasize that utilizing bamboo has a minimal effect on the environment, providing a socially responsible alternative to traditional tonewoods.

sections.title: Climate Impact
sections.content: As a highly sustainable material, bamboo is utilized by modern makers to respond to current ecological challenges in the Philippines. Its rapid growth and wide distribution make it a primary driver for a climate-conscious creative industry.

sections.title: Community Forestry
sections.content: The craft provides vital economic opportunities; for instance, King Flute provides employment and generates income for barangays in Quezon, while Musikawayan Malabon preserves a century-old Katipunero tradition, ensuring heritage and livelihood flow harmoniously together.
